meta.blurb: Elena makes one small mistake at work, and a cruel voice in her head will not stop. Her aunt invites her to a Thursday circle in the library, where she learns, step by step, how to be on her own side.
meta.bible: Elena Costa: a translator in her thirties who works from home; careful, shy and hard on herself. Rosa Costa: her aunt, who once ran a small flower shop for six years; she leads the Thursday circle; wise, humorous and gentle. Walter: a retired bus driver and churchgoer in the circle. Hana: a young Muslim student in the circle. Dev: a quiet man in the circle. Mr Hartley: Elena's client, who replies kindly. Millbrook Library: where the Thursday circle meets in the back room, with tea and biscuits. Ideas and traditions, each correctly attributed and treated with respect: Metta, loving-kindness, an early Buddhist practice in the Pali language, and an early Buddhist text in which a king finds that no one is dearer to him than himself; Hillel and the Pirkei Avot, a Jewish collection of ethical sayings: if I am not for myself, who will be for me; the Christian and Jewish command to love your neighbour as yourself; the hadith, a saying recorded of the Prophet Muhammad that the body has a right over you; Guilt versus Shame; Perfectionism; Boundaries; Common humanity. Research on self-kindness is described as suggestive and still growing, never as settled. The three questions: what am I feeling, what do I need, what would I say to a friend. Radical comes from the Latin word for root.  Voice and tone: warm, plain, gently funny, never preachy. Added for the full-length book: Marta: Elena's closest friend, a graphic designer who once lost a client's design file. Tomas Costa: Elena's father in Porto, Rosa's brother, an accountant; loving but hard, afraid for his daughter, proud of careful work. Ines Costa: Elena's mother. Miss Albright: the teacher who wrote careless on Elena's failed mathematics exam at fourteen, a red thirty-one. Maeve: a hospital nurse in the circle who works night shifts; she has a low season, sees her doctor and returns steadier. Mrs Osei: the librarian who unlocks the back room and later joins the circle. Mr Pike: a rude client of Elena's who pays late; Elena sets clear terms and he leaves. Mrs Pollard: Elena's formidable downstairs neighbour. Ms Vane: an editor at Larkfield Press who offers Elena a short Portuguese novel to translate, about one hundred and eighty pages, after Mr Hartley mentions her. Joel: a young father who joins the circle late. Ruth: Walter's late wife; Dev repairs her old watch. Green Door: Rosa's flower shop on Mill Lane, open six years, closed after a rent rise and a supermarket. Ada: Rosa's old friend who said an ending is not a failure. Salman and Abu Darda: two companions of the Prophet Muhammad in the hadith where the Prophet agrees that the body has a right over you. King Pasenadi of Kosala and Queen Mallika: the royal couple in the early Buddhist text. Hillel: a Jewish teacher of about two thousand years ago. Pirkei Avot: the Jewish collection of ethical sayings. Leviticus: the book of the Hebrew Bible with the command to love your neighbour as yourself, which Jesus names in the Gospels as the second of the two greatest commandments. Psalm 139: fearfully and wonderfully made. Tawba: the Arabic word for repentance, which carries the sense of returning. Rahma: the Arabic word for mercy. The Inspector: Elena's name for her inner critic, a small stern figure with folded arms and a clipboard. Cornflowers: seeds Rosa gives Elena; one blooms blue in winter. Millbrook Park: the park beside the library, with a worn path across the grass. Porto and the Douro valley: Portuguese places; Elena translates from Portuguese into English. Larkfield Press: the publisher. Saudade: a Portuguese word for longing. Mr Hartley imports cork and wine from Portugal; he is away for two months after the contract is sent, then signs the corrected contract and sends a postcard of cork oaks. The circle meets on Thursday evenings through one autumn and says each season that it is not therapy. Help beats: the signs that more help is needed, and the advice to speak to a doctor, a counsellor or a crisis line, are in beats 153 to 157, and again in beats 199 and 200. The book offers general ideas only, not treatment and not medical advice. Original wording only; no branded terms from any other book are used.

beats.scene: Elena stares at a contract on her laptop with a hand over her mouth
beats.summary: Elena, a translator, sends an important contract to a client and then spots a wrong number in it.

beats.scene: A finger rests on a circled figure on a bright laptop screen
beats.summary: She checks the file and finds forty-one thousand where the Portuguese original says fourteen thousand.

beats.scene: A shadowy figure points a finger over Elena's shoulder in a dim room
beats.summary: A cruel voice in her head begins to scold her.

beats.scene: A long paper scroll of old mistakes unrolls across a dim floor
beats.summary: The voice lists her old slips and predicts that every client will hear of this one.

beats.scene: A laptop shows an out-of-office message beside a cooling mug of tea
beats.summary: Mr Hartley's automatic reply says he is away for two months, and Elena decides to wait until she feels calm.

beats.scene: Elena holds a phone to her ear and smiles a tight smile
beats.summary: Her friend Marta phones about Saturday's dinner, and Elena says everything is fine.

beats.scene: Two friends sit across a cafe table, one white-faced, one pouring tea
beats.summary: After the call Elena remembers comforting Marta when Marta lost an important file.

beats.scene: Two mugs of tea sit side by side, one steaming and one cold
beats.summary: Elena realises she would never speak to Marta the way she speaks to herself.

beats.scene: A woman lies awake in a dark bedroom staring at the ceiling
beats.summary: At night the voice replays the mistake again and again.

beats.scene: Elena in a dressing gown holds a phone beside a sunny kitchen window
beats.summary: Her aunt Rosa phones, hears how tired she sounds, and invites her to the Thursday circle at the library.

beats.scene: A woman climbs library steps at dusk with her collar turned up
beats.summary: Elena goes to Millbrook Library on Thursday, nearly turns back, and Mrs Osei leads her to the back room.

beats.scene: Six people sit in a circle with mugs of tea
beats.summary: Elena meets the circle: Rosa, Walter, Hana, Dev and Maeve.

beats.scene: Rosa pours tea beside a whiteboard with three short rules
beats.summary: Rosa explains the circle: no experts, one idea a week, one small thing to try, nobody has to speak.

beats.scene: Hands rise slowly around a circle while one man laughs
beats.summary: Rosa asks who is hard on themselves, and every hand goes up.

beats.scene: Rosa writes the word kindness in marker on a whiteboard
beats.summary: The week's idea: kindness towards yourself is not selfishness, laziness or weakness.

beats.scene: An older man in a cardigan frowns with his arms folded
beats.summary: Walter objects: he was raised to think that thinking of yourself was close to a sin, and Rosa asks about firm and kind coaches.

beats.scene: A young woman in a headscarf holds a mug and speaks gently
beats.summary: Hana says a good person in her family gives to everyone; Rosa says a well that is never filled runs dry.

beats.scene: A shelf of psychology books glows under a reading lamp
beats.summary: Rosa says some research suggests self-kindness helps people try again after failure, but the research is still growing.

beats.scene: Elena writes in a small notebook under a lamp
beats.summary: Rosa sets the week's task: notice the harsh voice and write down its exact words.

beats.scene: Streetlamps glow along a wet pavement as a woman walks home
beats.summary: Elena walks home doubtful but curious and writes the first words of the voice in her notebook.

beats.scene: A notebook page filled with harsh words, some crossed out
beats.summary: During the week Elena fills a page with the voice's exact words and sees how repetitive and unimaginative it is.

beats.scene: A king and a queen talk quietly on a palace roof at sunset
beats.summary: Rosa tells the old Buddhist story of King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika, and the question he asks her.

beats.scene: A king in simple robes kneels before a seated teacher under a tree
beats.summary: The king admits the same, goes to the Buddha and tells him, and the Buddha answers with a verse.

beats.scene: An open palm-leaf manuscript lies beside a candle
beats.summary: The verse concludes that since everyone holds themselves dear, one who loves oneself should harm no one.

beats.scene: Rosa holds a small candle while the circle listens
beats.summary: Rosa explains metta, a Pali word for goodwill, a practice of silently offering good wishes to yourself and then others.

beats.scene: A quiet man looks down at his hands while others listen
beats.summary: Dev asks what to do if he feels nothing, and Rosa says to feel nothing, kindly.

beats.scene: Six people sit with eyes closed in lamplight, mugs on the floor
beats.summary: The circle tries the practice together for three minutes.

beats.scene: A woman peeks through one eye at a room of closed eyes
beats.summary: Elena feels ridiculous, opens one eye and sees Walter peeking too.

beats.scene: A woman sits on her bed whispering with her eyes closed
beats.summary: At home Elena whispers the phrases, may I be safe, may I be well, may I be at ease.

beats.scene: A woman sits very still as lamplight falls on her shoulders
beats.summary: On the third night something small changes: her shoulders drop, and she wants to say the words again.

beats.scene: Rosa rests a hand flat on her chest and smiles
beats.summary: Rosa shows a hand on the heart and says gentle touch may calm the body, though it does not suit everyone.

beats.scene: A nurse in a lanyard sits alone in a hospital staff room
beats.summary: Maeve says she tried the gesture alone in the staff room on a night shift and her breathing slowed.

beats.scene: Elena sits with one hand on her chest and her eyes closed
beats.summary: Elena tries the gesture in the circle and notices her palm's warmth and her own heartbeat.

beats.scene: Elena at her desk with one hand on her chest and a glowing laptop
beats.summary: At her desk with the contract still uncorrected, she tries the gesture and the voice returns louder.

beats.scene: A small anxious watchman stands guard at a locked gate at night
beats.summary: Rosa explains that the inner critic usually thinks it is protecting you, like an anxious watchman.

beats.scene: A woman at a desk nods politely toward an empty chair
beats.summary: Rosa teaches a short reply, thank you, I hear you, I will decide; Hana says her critic sounds like her old landlord.

beats.scene: A small stern figure with folded arms stands behind a chair
beats.summary: Elena pictures her critic as the Inspector, a small stern figure with folded arms and a clipboard.

beats.scene: Rosa hands out sheets of paper and pens around the circle
beats.summary: Rosa sets the next task: write yourself a short letter as a kind friend would.

beats.scene: A handwritten letter beginning Dear Elena lies on a kitchen table
beats.summary: Elena writes to herself about the contract in the words she once used for Marta.

beats.scene: A folded letter rests inside a desk drawer beside a pair of gloves
beats.summary: Reading the letter aloud, Elena cries, then folds it into a drawer to read again.

beats.scene: Rosa writes the words everyone makes mistakes on a whiteboard
beats.summary: On the fourth Thursday Rosa explains common humanity: the loneliness of failing, and the fact that everyone struggles.

beats.scene: A red bus rolls up a motorway ramp past astonished drivers
beats.summary: Walter tells how he once drove the number nine bus onto the motorway by mistake.

beats.scene: A watchmaker's bench with tiny gears and a single leftover screw
beats.summary: Dev, who repairs watches, tells of rebuilding an old watch and finding one screw left over.

beats.scene: A student stares at an exam paper with a worried frown
beats.summary: Hana says that in her first university exam she wrote a perfect answer to the wrong question.

beats.scene: Nurses gather around a table with a clipboard and calm faces
beats.summary: Maeve explains that hospitals discuss mistakes openly so that everyone can learn, without blaming one person.

beats.scene: Elena looks around a circle of faces lit by a lamp
beats.summary: Elena realises that everyone in the circle has a worst mistake and is still a kind, useful person.

beats.scene: Rosa speaks warmly with open hands in lamplight
beats.summary: Rosa says that struggling is part of being human, not proof that you are broken.

beats.scene: A desk drawer stands slightly open, full of crumpled drafts
beats.summary: Rosa says that everyone you admire has a drawer of mistakes that you never see.

beats.scene: Elena holds a phone with a small smile and a mug of tea
beats.summary: Elena finally tells Marta about the contract, and Marta quotes Elena's own words back to her.

beats.scene: A laptop with an unsent email glows on a dark desk
beats.summary: The Inspector is quieter, but the contract still has its wrong number, and Elena suspects that kindness has something to say about that.

beats.scene: Rosa places three small cards on a table beside a lamp
beats.summary: On the fifth Thursday Rosa brings sayings from other traditions and asks everyone to listen with respect and not to rank them.

beats.scene: An old man opens a worn Bible in a pool of lamplight
beats.summary: Walter reads the command to love your neighbour as yourself, from Leviticus and repeated by Jesus in the Gospels.

beats.scene: An older man sits with folded hands in quiet lamplight
beats.summary: Walter admits he read only half the sentence for years, until a minister told him it says as yourself, not instead of yourself.

beats.scene: An open Bible rests in lamplight beside a cup of tea
beats.summary: Walter reads a line from Psalm 139 saying that a person is fearfully and wonderfully made.

beats.scene: An old scroll unrolls beside a lamp and a mug
beats.summary: Rosa, as a respectful guest, reads Hillel's saying from Pirkei Avot: if I am not for myself, who will be for me.

beats.scene: Three lanterns hang in a row in a dark room
beats.summary: Rosa explains the three questions: be on your own side, care about others too, and begin now.

beats.scene: A young woman in a headscarf speaks with one hand open
beats.summary: Hana tells the hadith of Salman and Abu Darda, in which the Prophet agrees that the body has a right over you.

beats.scene: Gold calligraphy catches the light on a dark wall hanging
beats.summary: Hana says mercy is at the heart of her faith, since nearly every chapter of the Qur'an opens by naming God the Compassionate, the Merciful.

beats.scene: Dev raises a hand while teacups steam on the table
beats.summary: Dev asks whether all the sayings mean the same; Rosa says no, they have their own reasons but share a tune.

beats.scene: A notebook page with four words underlined in pencil
beats.summary: Elena writes on my own side in her notebook, words she cannot yet say aloud.

beats.scene: Two sentences are written one beneath the other on a whiteboard
beats.summary: On the sixth Thursday Rosa writes two sentences on the board: I did something wrong, and I am something wrong.

beats.scene: A signpost points two ways, to a mended fence and to a closed door
beats.summary: Rosa explains that guilt points at the act and leads to repair, while shame points at the self and makes us hide.

beats.scene: Elena sits very still with a hand over her mouth in lamplight
beats.summary: Elena realises that shame is why she has hidden the mistake for nearly six weeks.

beats.scene: A woman carries a broken chair to a workbench beside a toolbox
beats.summary: Rosa says kindness is not pretending nothing happened: real self-kindness includes taking responsibility.

beats.scene: Rosa writes three short lines on the whiteboard under a lamp
beats.summary: Rosa gives a recipe for a plain apology: say what happened, say you are sorry, say what you will do, and stop.

beats.scene: A woman deletes lines from an email, one hand on her chest
beats.summary: Elena drafts the email three times, deletes two grovelling versions, and puts a hand on her heart before the third.

beats.scene: A finger hovers over a send button in the evening light
beats.summary: She corrects the figure, attaches the fixed contract, writes a plain apology and sends it.

beats.scene: A woman walks a leafy park path with her hands in her pockets
beats.summary: While she waits the voice predicts disaster, and Elena goes for a long walk.

beats.scene: A phone screen shows a short, kind reply sent from a hotel
beats.summary: Mr Hartley replies from a hotel abroad: thanks for catching it, he would rather have it right, and he once ordered the wrong wine.

beats.scene: Elena sits on the stairs with a phone in her lap, laughing
beats.summary: The world has not ended; Elena laughs on the stairs, and plans to tell the circle.

beats.scene: Elena sleeps on a sofa under a blanket beside a cold cup of tea
beats.summary: After the relief Elena crashes with tiredness and sees that she has been working late for months.

beats.scene: Rosa pours tea beside a clock that shows a late hour
beats.summary: Rosa says tiredness makes the critic louder, and that poor sleep is linked with low mood, though everyone differs.

beats.scene: A nurse drinks tea at a window while the city is dark
beats.summary: Maeve says the critic is loudest at four in the morning, and she never judges her life at that hour.

beats.scene: A bedside lamp clicks off beside a clock showing eleven
beats.summary: Elena tries lights out by eleven for a week, and answers guilt that sleeping is not wasting time.

beats.scene: Rosa draws a circle with a small gate on a whiteboard
beats.summary: Rosa introduces boundaries: a line that shows where you end, and saying no kindly can be self-kindness.

beats.scene: A man in a cardigan leans over a table, pretending to bark orders
beats.summary: Elena describes Mr Pike, who sends work late on Friday for Monday, and Walter offers to play him so she can practise saying no.

beats.scene: Elena and an older man face each other, he waving a rolled newspaper
beats.summary: In the role play Walter overacts, and Elena laughs and finds the words: Wednesday is possible, Monday is not.

beats.scene: A short polite email on a laptop beside a calendar with Wednesday circled
beats.summary: Elena sends Mr Pike a polite reply offering Wednesday, and he agrees; nothing terrible happens.

beats.scene: A watchmaker's bench stacked with dozens of waiting watches
beats.summary: Dev confesses he has never said no and has too many watches waiting; he practises let me think about it and I will get back to you.

beats.scene: A woman closes a laptop and opens a window onto an evening park
beats.summary: Rosa says every no is also a yes to something else; Elena says yes to a long walk with her phone off.

beats.scene: A laptop screen shows the same paragraph typed in many small variations
beats.summary: Elena rewrites one paragraph of a hotel brochure eleven times at midnight and recognises perfectionism.

beats.scene: Rosa holds up two pencils, one sharp and one worn, to the light
beats.summary: Rosa says high standards are fine, but the test is whether a standard helps you do better or only makes you feel small.

beats.scene: A hand-tied bouquet of mixed flowers sits on a shop counter
beats.summary: Rosa tells how no bouquet in her flower shop was perfect, yet customers loved them: good enough is often good.

beats.scene: A student sits among colour-coded notebooks and highlighter pens
beats.summary: Hana admits she spent hours decorating her notes and learned to stop when a page is ready, not flawless.

beats.scene: A finished hotel brochure lies open beside an empty coffee cup
beats.summary: Elena allows two careful readings, sends the brochure at good enough, and the hotel owner is delighted.

beats.scene: A phone screen shows a smiling woman holding up a golden prize
beats.summary: Elena sees a post about another translator winning a prize, feels small, and the Inspector starts to compare them.

beats.scene: A lit window glows in a dark street with a shadowed room behind it
beats.summary: Rosa says we compare our insides with other people's outsides, which is an unfair contest.

beats.scene: A photograph of bright tomatoes with a collapsing shed just outside the frame
beats.summary: Walter shows a photo of his prize tomatoes and describes the shed and weeds just outside the frame.

beats.scene: A woman holds a pencil above a page headed what I want
beats.summary: Rosa suggests asking envy what it points to; Elena sees that she wants to translate books, not only contracts.

beats.scene: A notebook page headed one day holds a single line of handwriting
beats.summary: Elena writes that she would like to translate a book one day, as a wish and not a test.

beats.scene: Elena holds a phone in a dim kitchen while a crisp voice speaks
beats.summary: Elena phones her father Tomas in Porto on his birthday, and he asks whether she is still only translating contracts.

beats.scene: A woman paces a dim kitchen with her arms wrapped around herself
beats.summary: After the call Elena wants to scrub the feeling away or scold herself for being so sensitive.

beats.scene: Rosa places an open hand gently over a closed fist
beats.summary: Rosa teaches that you can make room for hard feelings and say: this hurts, and it makes sense that it hurts.

beats.scene: Two arrows lie on the ground, one near a shield and one beyond
beats.summary: Rosa recalls the Buddhist teaching of two arrows: the pain that life brings, and the second arrow of self-blame.

beats.scene: A woman at a kitchen table writes feeling words in a list
beats.summary: Elena names what she feels after the call: disappointed, lonely and a little angry; naming loosens the knot.

beats.scene: Rosa pins a card with three questions in large letters to the wall
beats.summary: Rosa gives the three questions: what am I feeling, what do I need, and what would I say to a friend.

beats.scene: Elena sits by a window with a card in her hand and a mug
beats.summary: Elena asks the three questions about her father's call: hurt, needs to be seen, and his words are not a measure of her.

beats.scene: A page covered in red corrections lies beside a laptop
beats.summary: Mr Pike returns her Wednesday translation with a long list of corrections, some fair and some rude, and Elena wants to give up.

beats.scene: A page divided into two columns, true and useful, ruled in pencil
beats.summary: Rosa teaches the pause before answering criticism: ask what is true and what is useful; Elena sorts Mr Pike's list.

beats.scene: A short calm reply on a screen beside a tidy desk
beats.summary: She fixes the two real errors, ignores the tone, sends a calm reply, and notes that she stayed on her own side.

beats.scene: Six people write quietly with pencils in a lamplit room
beats.summary: Rosa asks whose voice the inner critic sounds like and gives ten minutes of silent writing.

beats.scene: A girl in school uniform looks at a mathematics paper with a red mark
beats.summary: Elena remembers failing a mathematics exam at fourteen, with a red thirty-one and the word careless from Miss Albright.

beats.scene: A girl sits at a dinner table opposite a silent man
beats.summary: At dinner her father looks at the paper in silence and says she will have to be twice as careful.

beats.scene: A notebook page with the word careless circled many times
beats.summary: Elena realises that careless was the first word the voice used about the contract: it was Miss Albright's word in her father's tone.

beats.scene: Rosa sits with her hands on her knees as lamplight catches her glasses
beats.summary: Rosa says we absorb voices from parents, teachers and society, and understanding where a voice came from is not blaming anyone.

beats.scene: A grown woman sits beside a girl in uniform on a school bench
beats.summary: Rosa guides a short imagining and says anyone may stop; Elena pictures herself beside her fourteen-year-old self.

beats.scene: A woman puts a gentle arm around a girl's shoulders on a bench
beats.summary: Elena tells the girl in her mind that one exam cannot measure her and that she is already loved.

beats.scene: A note in a grown-up hand lies open in a notebook on a desk
beats.summary: Elena opens her eyes, forgives her younger self and writes her a short note.

beats.scene: A woman eats from a paper bag of sweets on a park bench
beats.summary: On the way home Elena buys the sour cherry sweets she loved at fourteen and eats them on a bench by the pond.

beats.scene: A woman sleeps peacefully while a small figure waits beside the door
beats.summary: Elena sleeps deeply; the Inspector is still there but now sounds like an echo of other people's old fears.

beats.scene: A woman stacks chairs beside an older woman in an empty library room
beats.summary: After the meeting Elena helps Rosa stack the chairs and asks about the flower shop she once ran.

beats.scene: A small shopfront with a green door and buckets of tulips
beats.summary: Rosa describes the Green Door, the little flower shop she ran for six years and loved.

beats.scene: A tired woman arranges flowers by lamplight before dawn
beats.summary: Rosa worked from dawn to night and was kind to every customer but cruel to herself; she once apologised to a rose.

beats.scene: A shopfront with a closed sign and empty buckets in the rain
beats.summary: In the sixth year the rent rose and a supermarket began selling cheap flowers, and the Green Door closed.

beats.scene: A woman sits alone at a kitchen table with the curtains closed
beats.summary: Afterwards Rosa treated the closing as proof that she was a failure and crossed the road to avoid the shop.

beats.scene: Two women sit side by side on a bench sharing a flask of tea
beats.summary: Her friend Ada sits with her and says the shop ended but Rosa did not fail at flowers: an ending and a failure are different things.

beats.scene: A woman reads in a library armchair beside a small stack of books
beats.summary: Rosa spent her days in Millbrook Library, found a book about loving-kindness and later began the Thursday circle in that room.

beats.scene: A woman stands at a window at dusk with one hand on her chest
beats.summary: Rosa admits she still has bad days, especially when the shop's anniversary comes, and she is not a finished teacher.

beats.scene: Two women sit on stacked chairs, one with a hand on the other's arm
beats.summary: Elena sees her calm aunt as a person who has struggled too, and says she is glad to know her better.

beats.scene: A small paper packet of seeds rests on an open palm
beats.summary: Rosa gives Elena a packet of cornflower seeds saved from the shop, and Elena sows them in a pot and forgets them.

beats.scene: A glass of water, a bowl of soup and an open door
beats.summary: Rosa says self-kindness is not only a feeling but plain actions such as water, food, daylight and sleep.

beats.scene: A woman eats soup at a table with a closed laptop beside her
beats.summary: Elena sees that she forgets to eat until four o'clock, and starts eating lunch at a table with the laptop closed.

beats.scene: A woman in a coat walks beneath trees with a robin on a fence
beats.summary: Elena begins a short morning walk to the park and notices small things, including a robin who seems to wait for her.

beats.scene: A man sits at a cafe window with a cup and a small notebook
beats.summary: Dev has begun to buy himself a proper coffee every Saturday and drink it slowly at a cafe window.

beats.scene: A child's pencil map is pinned beside a pot of coloured pencils
beats.summary: Rosa says kindness also needs play and joy, and asks what each of them loved to do at ten years old.

beats.scene: A pencil drawing of a street map with tiny trees and a pond
beats.summary: Elena remembers drawing maps of imaginary towns at ten, and draws a map of her own street for the joy of it.

beats.scene: A grown man glues a tiny wheel onto a model red bus
beats.summary: Walter confesses that he has built model buses for thirty years, and has stopped feeling ashamed of it.

beats.scene: A young woman at an open window raises her hands in the dawn light
beats.summary: Hana begins each morning with a short prayer of thanks, and notices she feels grateful for her body before she can criticise it.

beats.scene: A woman stands before a bathroom mirror with a hand on her shoulder
beats.summary: Rosa suggests thanking the body for what it does, not judging its looks; Elena tries at the mirror and feels awkward.

beats.scene: Two hands rest above a keyboard in warm lamplight
beats.summary: Elena thanks her hands for almost ten years of typing other people's words.

beats.scene: A woman holds a door open for a mother with a pram
beats.summary: Elena notices she is more patient with others: she waits calmly in a queue and holds a door for a pram.

beats.scene: A woman at a front door speaks calmly to a scowling older neighbour
beats.summary: Her downstairs neighbour Mrs Pollard complains about footsteps, and Elena listens, says sorry once and offers a rug.

beats.scene: Two friends laugh at a cafe table with a large slice of lemon cake
beats.summary: Marta says Elena seems softer and lighter, and Elena says she is practising being on her own side.

beats.scene: Rosa stands beside a whiteboard that reads practice, not cure
beats.summary: Rosa warns that self-kindness is a practice, not a cure, and that terrible weeks do not mean the practice has failed.

beats.scene: A tree with deep roots is drawn in chalk on a blackboard
beats.summary: Rosa explains that radical comes from the Latin word for root: radical kindness goes to the root and stays there when we fail.

beats.scene: A broken mug lies on a kitchen floor beside spilled tea
beats.summary: A crowded week arrives, Elena drops her favourite mug, and the Inspector returns at full volume.

beats.scene: A woman sits on a bed in the dark, head in hands
beats.summary: Elena spirals all evening, then is furious with herself for failing at kindness, which is only the Inspector in a new coat.

beats.scene: Rosa opens her arms with a smile as Elena enters the library room
beats.summary: On Thursday Elena confesses the bad day, and Rosa says welcome back: beginning again is the practice itself.

beats.scene: A woman bows her head over cupped hands in a quiet room
beats.summary: Hana says the Arabic word tawba, repentance, carries the sense of returning, and a person may return as often as needed.

beats.scene: A yellow note with two words is stuck to the edge of a laptop
beats.summary: Elena writes begin again on a sticky note and glues the broken mug back together.

beats.scene: A sturdy gate with a latch stands between a garden and a muddy lane
beats.summary: Rosa says self-kindness includes protecting yourself from people who mistreat you; gentleness is not putting up with everything.

beats.scene: A pile of unpaid invoices sits beside a calendar with red circles
beats.summary: Elena checks her records: Mr Pike pays late, writes rudely and has never said thank you.

beats.scene: Two gates in a garden fence, one wide open and one latched
beats.summary: Walter says a good boundary is a gate, not a wall: open to friends, shut to those who trample the flowers.

beats.scene: A short email on a screen under the heading new terms
beats.summary: Elena writes Mr Pike a short, clear email asking for payment within thirty days and three working days for each job.

beats.scene: An angry message glows on a phone beside a quiet cup of tea
beats.summary: Mr Pike replies in capital letters and takes his work elsewhere; Elena feels fear about money and, underneath, relief.

beats.scene: Morning sunlight falls across a woman sitting quietly on a chair

beats.scene: A woman sits by a window with a hand on her chest

beats.scene: An empty chair stands beside a mug of untouched tea

beats.scene: An older man holds a small framed photograph of a smiling woman

beats.scene: A wall clock beside a calendar with weeks crossed out

A1A2: Elena sent a contract to a client with a wrong number.
The number said forty-one thousand, but it should say fourteen thousand.
A cruel voice in her head said, you are useless.
The voice reminded her of every old mistake she had made.
Mr Hartley was away for two months, so she waited.
Her friend Marta called, and Elena said she was fine.
She remembered when Marta lost an important file at work.
Elena would never speak to a friend in that way.
That night she could not sleep, and the voice kept talking.
Aunt Rosa called and asked her to come on Thursday.
On Thursday Elena walked to the library, feeling nervous.
Six people sat in a circle with cups of tea.
Rosa said nobody had to speak, but everyone was welcome.
Rosa asked who in the room was hard on themselves.
Rosa said that kindness to yourself is not selfish or weak.
Walter said that thinking of himself had always felt wrong.
Hana said her family always gave to others and never rested.
Some studies say kindness to yourself helps you try again.
Rosa asked them to write down what their inner voice said.
Elena walked home and wrote one line in her notebook.
By Thursday her notebook page was full of cruel words.
Rosa told them an old story about a king and queen.
The king said that nobody was dearer to him either.
He said other people love themselves too, so we should not harm anyone.
Rosa taught them a quiet practice called metta.
Dev asked what to do if he feels nothing.
They closed their eyes and said the kind words together.
Elena felt silly and opened one eye to look around.
At home Elena said, quietly, may I be safe.
After a few tries, her shoulders felt a little softer.
Rosa showed them how to put a hand on the heart.
Maeve said she tried it on a night shift at work.
Elena put a hand on her heart and felt it beat.
At her desk, the voice came back, louder than before.
Rosa said the inner critic thinks it is protecting you.
Rosa said to thank the voice, but not to obey it.
Elena gave the voice a name: the Inspector.
Rosa asked them to write a kind letter to themselves.
Elena began her letter with the words Dear Elena.
Elena read the letter and her eyes filled with tears.
Rosa said that everyone makes mistakes and everyone struggles.
Walter once drove his bus onto the motorway by mistake.
Dev fixes watches, and once he had a screw left over.
Hana once answered the wrong question in an exam.
Maeve said that at work they talk about mistakes openly.
Elena saw that everyone in the room had made mistakes.
Rosa said that struggling does not mean you are broken.
Rosa said that everyone has a drawer full of mistakes.
Elena told Marta about the wrong number, and Marta smiled.
The voice was quieter now, but the contract still waited.
Rosa brought sayings from three old traditions to share.
Walter read the old words: love your neighbour as yourself.
Walter said he had always forgotten the last two words.
Walter also read a line that says people are wonderfully made.
Rosa read an old Jewish saying about being for yourself.
Rosa said you should be on your own side, but not only.
Hana told a story about a friend who rested too little.
Hana said that mercy is at the heart of her faith.
Dev asked if all the sayings meant the same thing.
Elena wrote a new phrase in her notebook: on my own side.
Rosa wrote two short sentences on the board.
Guilt is about what you did, and shame is about who you are.
Elena saw that shame had made her hide for weeks.
Rosa said that being kind does not mean pretending nothing happened.
Rosa said a good apology is short, plain and clear.
Elena wrote the email three times and threw away two.
She fixed the number, attached the file, and pressed send.
She waited for an answer, so she went for a walk.
Mr Hartley wrote back, and his message was kind.
The world had not ended, and Elena laughed out loud.
After the relief, Elena felt very tired and slept all afternoon.
Rosa said that when we are tired, the voice gets louder.
Maeve said that she never judges her life at four in the morning.
Elena turned off her light at eleven every night.
Rosa said that saying no can be a kind act.
Elena had a client who always wanted work by Monday.
Elena laughed and said, I can finish it on Wednesday.
Elena wrote to Mr Pike, and he said yes to Wednesday.
Dev said he could never say no to anyone.
Rosa said every no is also a yes to something else.
Elena wrote the same small paragraph eleven times that night.
Rosa said high standards are good, but cruel standards are not.
Rosa said that good enough is often really good.
Hana spent hours making her study notes look beautiful.
Elena read it twice, then sent it to the hotel.
Elena saw that another translator had won a big prize.
Rosa said we compare our insides with other people's outsides.
Walter showed them a photo of his fine tomatoes.
Elena saw that she wanted to translate books, not contracts.
Elena wrote in her notebook, one day I will translate a book.
Elena phoned her father, and his words made her sad.
Elena tried to push the sad feeling away.
Rosa said you can say, this really hurts, and that makes sense.
Rosa spoke of two arrows: the pain and the blame.
Elena wrote a list of her feelings on paper.
Rosa gave the circle three questions to ask themselves.
Elena used the three questions on her father's call.
Mr Pike sent back her work with a list of errors.
Rosa taught them to ask of criticism, is this true and useful?
She fixed two real mistakes and sent a calm reply.
Rosa asked whose voice the inner critic sounds like.
Elena remembered a school test that she had failed.
Her father said that she must be twice as careful.
Elena saw that the voice used the same word, careless.
Rosa said the inner critic often uses other people's words.
Elena imagined that she sat next to herself at fourteen.
Elena told her, one test does not decide who you are.
Elena opened her eyes and said sorry to the girl she had been.
On the way home Elena bought sweets and sat on a bench.
That night Elena slept well, and the voice was quiet.
Elena helped Rosa stack chairs and asked about her shop.
Rosa said her shop had a green door and many flowers.
Rosa worked from early morning until late at night.
After six years, the little shop had to close.
Rosa told herself that she was a complete failure.
Her friend Ada said the shop had ended, but Rosa had not failed.
Rosa went to the library and found a book about kindness.
Rosa said that she still had bad days too.
Elena saw her calm aunt in a new way.
Rosa gave Elena a small packet of flower seeds.
Rosa said that kindness can be water, food and fresh air.
Elena ate lunch at a table, away from her laptop.
Every morning Elena walked to the park near her home.
Dev said he now buys himself a good coffee on Saturdays.
Rosa asked what they had loved to do when they were ten.
Elena drew a map of her street with a pencil.
Walter said he builds small model buses at home.
Hana begins each day with a short prayer of thanks.
Elena thanked her legs for carrying her through the day.
Elena thanked her hands for all the years of work.
Elena let a woman with a baby go first.
A neighbour complained about noise, and Elena stayed calm.
Marta said, you seem softer and lighter these days.
Rosa said that kindness is a practice, not a cure.
Rosa said the word radical means going to the root.
Elena dropped her favourite cup and it broke into pieces.
That night she was angry because she could not be kind.
Rosa smiled and said, welcome back, and begin again.
Hana said that in her faith, you can always return.
Elena wrote begin again on a small yellow note.
Rosa said that you may protect yourself from people who are cruel.
Elena counted how late Mr Pike had paid her.
Walter said that a gate can be open or closed.
Elena sent Mr Pike a short email about new rules.
Mr Pike was angry, and he took his work elsewhere.
Rosa suggested five quiet minutes of sitting each day.
In the first week her thoughts would not stay quiet.
One morning, her five minutes were calm and quiet.
Rosa said that good wishes can grow wider and wider.
Elena wished Mr Pike well, though it was not easy.
Maeve did not come to the circle for two weeks.
Maeve said she had felt very low for many months.
Rosa said that these practices are not a treatment.
Maeve said that she had already been to see her doctor.
Rosa said that when pain is heavy, you should ask for help.
Dev said that he sees a counsellor, and it helps.
Elena decided to see a doctor if she felt very low for weeks.
Elena told the circle her whole story, from the start.
Walter spoke about his wife Ruth, who had died.
Elena saw a notice that said, new members welcome.
A publisher asked Elena to translate a whole novel.
The old voice said, they chose the wrong person.
Elena asked herself the three questions about the offer.
Rosa said, you will not do it perfectly, and that is fine.
Elena worked on the book every morning, slowly and well.
One Portuguese word had no good word in English.
She found a mistake in a chapter she had already sent.
She put a hand on her heart and took a slow breath.
Elena told Ms Vane about the mistake, and the reply was kind.
This time it took twenty minutes, not six weeks.
Rosa said that kindness is a path we make by walking.
Elena saw a path that people had made across the grass.
Rosa said that repeating a habit makes it easier.
Elena made a plan with three small steps for each day.
Elena wrote her three steps on a card for her desk.
Elena missed two days, and then she began again.
Elena had lunch with Rosa and said thank you.
Rosa said, I only held the door, and you walked through.
Elena told her father about the book she would translate.
Elena saw small green plants growing in the pot by her window.
Four new people came, and the room felt full.
Hana led the circle for the first time that evening.
Dev gave Walter a small watch that he had fixed.
Walter put the watch on his wrist and smiled.
Maeve told them that she was feeling much better.
Elena showed a new member how to ask the three questions.
Elena learned more about kindness by helping someone else.
Rosa said that the last meeting was nearly here.
Rosa wrote five short lessons on a large sheet of paper.
Each person wrote a kind note to someone else.
Snow began to fall as the circle said goodbye.
Mr Hartley came home and signed the contract with the right number.
Elena finished the first part of the book and sent it.
She found a small mistake, and she did not panic.
Elena and Rosa walked together through the snowy park.
One blue flower opened in the pot on her window.
Elena wrote a kind letter to herself for next year.
Elena thought about the root of everything she had learned.
Rosa's card said, read the old words for yourself.

B1B2: Elena Costa is a translator, and she works from a small desk at home. This morning she sent an important contract to a client, and she has just seen a wrong number in it.
She opened the file and read page three again, slowly, with her finger on the screen. The Portuguese original said fourteen thousand, but her English said forty-one thousand.
At once a voice in her head began to scold her. It said that she was careless, that she was a fraud, and that everyone would soon know.
It brought up a spelling mistake from years ago, a late invoice and a missed call. Then it promised her that Mr Hartley would warn every other client in the city.
She began an email to Mr Hartley, but his automatic reply said he was away for two months. She told herself to wait until she felt calm enough to explain, and her tea went cold beside the keyboard.
In the afternoon her friend Marta phoned to talk about Saturday's dinner. Elena put on a bright voice and said that everything was fine.
After the call, Elena remembered a morning two years ago when Marta had lost an important design file. She had sat beside her, made her a cup of tea and said that anyone could make such a mistake.
Then a strange question came to her, and she could not put it down. Why was she so gentle with Marta and so cruel with herself?
That night she lay awake, and the voice played the same morning over and over. Each time it ended in the same way, with Elena as the guilty one.
In the morning her aunt Rosa phoned and heard at once that something was wrong. She did not ask for details, but she invited Elena to a small evening circle at the library on Thursday.
On Thursday evening Elena almost turned back twice on the way to Millbrook Library. At the door the librarian, Mrs Osei, smiled and led her to the back room.
Rosa hugged her and introduced the others: Walter, Hana, Dev and Maeve. Elena took a chair near the door, just in case.
Rosa explained that there were no experts in the room. Each week they looked at one idea, tried one small thing and talked only if they wanted to.
Rosa asked how many of them were hard on themselves. Every hand went up, and Walter laughed loudly and said that he held the world record.
The idea for the first evening was a simple one, and Rosa wrote it on the board. Being kind to yourself, she said, is not selfish, lazy or weak, even though many people fear that it is.
Walter frowned and said that he had been raised to think of others first. He had learned that thinking of himself was almost a sin.
Hana said that in her family a good person gives to everyone and asks for nothing. Rosa answered gently that a well which is never filled will one day run dry.
Rosa said that some research points in a hopeful direction. People who treat themselves kindly after a failure seem more willing to try again, although the research is still growing.
Rosa gave them one small task for the week. They were to notice the harsh voice in their heads and write down its exact words, without arguing with it.
Walking home under the streetlamps, Elena was not convinced, but she was curious. At her kitchen table she opened a notebook and wrote the first words the voice had said.
All week Elena wrote down what the voice said, and by Wednesday she had filled a whole page. She noticed that it used the same few cruel words again and again.
On the second Thursday Rosa told them an old story from the Buddhist tradition. A king named Pasenadi sat on his palace roof with his queen, Mallika, and asked her a surprising question.
The king replied that no one was dearer to him than himself either. Struck by this, he went to the Buddha and told him what they had said.
The verse goes on to say that other people hold themselves just as dear. So a person who loves himself or herself should not harm others.
Rosa described metta, a word from the old Pali language that means goodwill or friendliness. In the practice you quietly offer good wishes to yourself first and then to other people.
Dev spoke for the first time and asked what to do if he felt nothing at all. Rosa smiled and said that then you feel nothing, as kindly as you can.
Rosa led them through three minutes of quiet practice, with their mugs on the floor. She spoke the old phrases slowly, and each person repeated them silently in their own mind.
Elena felt ridiculous, as if she were acting in a play. She opened one eye and saw that Walter had opened one eye too.
That night Elena tried some of the traditional phrases at home. She whispered, “May I be safe, may I be well, may I be at ease,” and the words sounded thin in the quiet room.
Nothing dramatic happened, but on the third night her shoulders dropped a little. She noticed that she wanted to say the words one more time.
On the third Thursday Rosa showed them how to rest a hand on the chest. She said that some research suggests gentle touch can calm the body, but it is not comfortable for everyone.
Maeve said that she had tried it during a night shift in the hospital staff room. For two minutes she had felt her breathing slow down.
Elena felt self-conscious at first, but she rested her hand on her chest anyway. She noticed the warmth of her palm and the slow rise and fall of her own breathing.
On Friday morning she sat at her desk and tried the gesture while the contract file stayed open. The voice came back at once, louder than before, and said that this was a waste of time.

At the next meeting Elena described what had happened at her desk, and she sounded rather discouraged. Rosa said that the inner critic usually believes it is protecting you, like an anxious watchman who shouts at every small sound.
Rosa taught them a short reply: thank you, I hear you, and I will decide. Hana laughed and said that her critic sounded exactly like her old landlord.
At home Elena imagined her critic as a small, stern figure with folded arms and a clipboard. She named it the Inspector, and it looked much less powerful standing behind a chair.
Rosa handed out paper and pens and asked them to write a short letter to themselves. It should be written as a kind friend would write it, not as a judge.
Elena began, “Dear Elena, I saw what happened with the contract, and I know how much it hurt.” Then she wrote for a page, using the words she had used for Marta.
When she read the letter aloud, her voice shook and her eyes filled with tears. She folded it carefully and put it in a drawer where she could find it again.
On the fourth Thursday Rosa talked about the feeling of being the only person who fails. She called the opposite of that feeling common humanity, the simple fact that everyone struggles.
Walter told them that he had once taken the number nine bus onto the motorway by mistake. Thirty passengers had enjoyed a very long and surprising ride, and he had felt like a fool for a week.
Dev said that he repaired watches for a living, and he told them a quiet story. He had once rebuilt an old watch and found one tiny screw left over on his bench.
Hana said that in her first university exam she had written a perfect answer to the wrong question. She had cried all the way home on the bus.
Maeve said that in many hospitals mistakes are discussed openly so that everyone can learn from them. The aim is not to blame one person, but to understand what went wrong and make the system safer.
Elena looked slowly around the circle and noticed something that she had not expected. Every person there had a worst mistake, and every one of them was still a kind and useful person.
Rosa said that struggling is part of being human and is not proof that something is wrong with you. It is the common condition of people, and it is the reason that kindness is needed at all.
Rosa said that every person you admire has a drawer full of mistakes that you never see. Most people show only the finished work and keep the rest out of sight.
At last Elena phoned Marta and told her about the contract. Marta was silent for a moment, and then she said, “You told me that anyone could make such a mistake.”
The Inspector was quieter now, but the contract still sat on her computer with its wrong number. Elena knew that something would have to be done about it, and soon.
On the fifth Thursday Rosa brought sayings from three old traditions. She asked everyone to listen with respect, not to compare or rank them, and to correct her if she got anything wrong.
Walter read the command to love your neighbour as yourself. It appears in the book of Leviticus, and in the Gospels Jesus names it as the second of the two greatest commandments.
Walter admitted that for years he had read only the first half of the sentence. His minister once told him that it says as yourself, not instead of yourself.
Walter added a line from Psalm 139, in which the writer says that he is fearfully and wonderfully made. He said that the verse had helped him on his hardest mornings.
Rosa read a saying of Hillel, a Jewish teacher who lived about two thousand years ago. It comes from Pirkei Avot, a collection of ethical sayings: if I am not for myself, who will be for me?

Rosa explained the three questions one at a time, and the circle listened closely. First you must stand on your own side, then you must care about others too, and you must begin today and not someday.
Hana told a story from the hadith, the recorded sayings of the Prophet Muhammad. A man named Salman urged his friend Abu Darda to eat and sleep, and the Prophet said that Salman was right.

Hana added that nearly every chapter of the Qur'an begins by naming God as the Compassionate, the Merciful. Her grandmother, she said, treated every guest like a king and herself like the last in line.
Dev asked quietly whether all these sayings meant the same thing. Rosa said that they did not, because each had its own reasons, but that they rhymed.
