Rosa smiled as though he had asked the best question of the night and told him that in that case he should feel nothing, as kindly as possible. The words, she said, were only an invitation, and a feeling that did not accept it on the first night was not a failure.

Rosa asked them to put their mugs on the floor, close their eyes if they wished, and sit for three minutes with their feet planted and their shoulders loose. She spoke the traditional phrases slowly, with long pauses between them, so that each person could repeat them silently or let them pass through like weather. The room became so quiet that Elena could hear the radiator ticking and, somewhere beyond the wall, a trolley of returned books rattling past.

Elena felt ridiculous within seconds, as though she had been handed a part in a play without being told the plot. She opened one eye to check whether everyone else was managing better, and she found Walter's one open eye already looking back at her with enormous dignity. They both closed their eyes again at once, and Elena had to press her lips together to stop a laugh that might, she suspected, have been the first honest feeling of her whole week.

At home that night Elena sat on her bed and tried the traditional phrases, which vary from teacher to teacher but always sound much the same. She whispered that she might be safe, might be well and might be at ease, and the words sounded thin in the empty room. Rosa had warned her that this awkwardness was normal, and that it usually fades with time.

Nothing dramatic happened, and she was almost relieved, because she would have distrusted anything dramatic. But on the third night, somewhere in the middle of the phrases, she noticed that her shoulders had dropped an inch from beside her ears and that her jaw had stopped clenching. It was a very small change, and yet she wanted to say the words once more, and she did.

On the third Thursday Rosa showed them a gesture that many people find soothing, which was simply to rest one hand flat on the centre of the chest and to feel its warmth. She said that some research suggests gentle touch can calm the body's stress response, although scientists are still working out the details and the effect is not the same for everyone. If the gesture felt wrong, she added, they could hold their own forearm, or simply wrap both hands around a warm mug.

Maeve, who worked nights on a busy hospital ward, said that she had tried the gesture alone in the staff room at about three o'clock in the morning. For two whole minutes, she said, she had felt her breathing slow and the hum of the vending machine fade into the background, and then a buzzer had sounded and the world had returned. Even so, she said, she had walked back to the ward with her shoulders a little lower than before.

Elena felt as self-conscious as a person dancing alone in a shop window, but she closed her eyes and rested her hand on her chest anyway. She noticed first the warmth of her palm through her jumper, and then, beneath it, the steady knock of her own heart, which had been working without complaint all through the terrible week. It struck her that she had never once thanked it, and that she had spent days shouting at the person it belonged to.

On Friday morning she sat at her desk with the wrongly numbered contract still open on the screen, and she tried the gesture there, in the very heart of the trouble. The voice came back at once, louder than before, to inform her that grown women with careers did not sit hugging themselves while important documents lay uncorrected. She dropped her hand, felt foolish and wondered whether the whole thing was a pleasant idea that fell apart when it met real life.

At the next meeting Elena described what had happened at her desk, and Rosa listened with every sign of delight, as though the voice's return were the best news of the week. She said that the inner critic is rarely a villain, and that it usually believes it is protecting us, like an anxious watchman who shouts at every small sound in case a thief is coming. Its methods are terrible, she said, but its motive is often to keep us safe from being rejected, laughed at or found out.

Rosa taught them a short reply that required no argument at all: thank you for your concern, I have heard you, and I will decide for myself. Hana laughed so suddenly that she nearly spilled her tea, and she said that her own critic sounded exactly like her old landlord, who also believed that he was only being helpful. The circle roared, and Elena noticed that when a harsh voice was given a face, even an unflattering one, it became considerably less frightening.

At home that evening Elena pictured her critic as a small, stern figure with folded arms and a clipboard, and she decided to call it the Inspector. Standing behind her chair with a pinched expression, it looked far less like the judge of her whole life and far more like an overworked official who had been given the wrong job. When it began its usual speech she said, in her head, thank you, I hear you, and she was startled to find that it paused.

For the week's practice Rosa handed out paper and pens and asked each of them to write a short letter to themselves about something they found hard. It was to be written as a kind friend would write it, someone who knew all the facts and still liked them very much, and not as a judge delivering a sentence. She told them that the letter did not have to be good, only honest and warm.

Elena began, with some embarrassment, “Dear Elena, I saw what happened with the contract, and I know how much it hurt.” She went on to say that one wrong number did not cancel nine years of careful work, that tired people make slips, and that the correction was a task rather than a trial. When she reached the end of the page she realised that she had used, almost word for word, the sentences she had once said to Marta.

When she read the letter aloud in the quiet flat, her voice shook halfway down the page, and she was astonished to find that she was crying. They were not unhappy tears exactly, but the tears of someone who has been spoken to kindly after a very long silence. She folded the pages carefully, put them in the top drawer of her desk, and decided that she would read them again whenever the Inspector grew too loud.

On the fourth Thursday Rosa spoke about a particular loneliness that comes with failure, the sense that everyone else is managing perfectly and that we alone are the exception. She called the remedy common humanity, which is only a grand name for the plain fact that to be a person is to make mistakes, to struggle and to be sometimes afraid. She suggested that the worst part of an error is often not the error itself but the feeling of being the only one.

Walter, whose booming laugh had softened, told them how he had once taken the number nine bus up the wrong slip road and onto the motorway, with thirty passengers on board and the next exit eleven miles away. A small boy at the front had cheered, an old lady had asked politely whether this was the scenic route, and Walter had wanted to sink through the floor. He had been ashamed for a week, and only years later did he understand that none of his passengers remembered it with anything but delight.

Dev, who repaired watches in a narrow shop near the station, finally spoke at length, and his voice was dry and shy and exact. He told them about the day he had rebuilt a customer's grandfather's watch and found, with the case already closed, a single tiny screw sitting accusingly on his bench. He had opened the watch again, put the screw where it belonged and spent the whole evening convinced that his career was a fraud.

Hana confessed that during her first university exam she had spent forty minutes writing a beautifully organised answer to a question that nobody had asked. She had only discovered it when the invigilator announced that there were five minutes left, and she had cried all the way home on the bus, convinced that she had thrown away her future. She had passed the course, as it happened, and the story now made her laugh until her headscarf slipped.

Maeve explained that on her ward, as in many hospitals and in aviation too, mistakes are discussed openly because a place where people hide their errors is a place where the same errors happen again. The aim, she said, is not to find one person to blame but to understand what went wrong and to build a safer system around everyone. She added with a tired smile that it was odd to be so kind to the whole team and so merciless to herself.

Elena looked slowly around the circle, at the lamp and the cooling tea and the faces, and noticed something she had not expected. Each of these people had a worst mistake, a story they replayed in the dark, and not one of them looked to her like a fraud or a failure. If anything they looked like exactly the sort of people she would trust with a spare key, which was a strange standard to apply to everyone but herself.

Rosa said that struggling is not a sign that something has gone wrong with you but a sign that you are alive and human, which is the one thing every person in the world has in common. Seen that way, she said, a mistake loses its power to isolate us, because it becomes a doorway into the company of everyone who has ever tried and failed. The circle was quiet for a moment, and then Walter said gruffly that this was a very large company indeed.

Rosa smiled and said that every person you admire has a drawer somewhere, packed with crumpled drafts, awkward emails and decisions they would undo if they could. We never see the drawer, she said, because people show us the finished work and keep the mess out of sight, and so we compare our private mess with everyone else's public polish. Elena thought of the crumpled drafts she had thrown away over the years, and for the first time they seemed to her less like evidence and more like a membership card.

On a quiet Saturday morning Elena phoned Marta and told her everything, from the wrong figure to the sleepless night to the cruel voice with its excellent memory. Marta listened without interrupting, and then she said that she had been waiting for weeks for Elena to stop saying she was fine. Anyone could make such a mistake, she added, as someone wise had once told her in a cafe, and Elena laughed and cried at the same time, which seemed to her an efficient use of a morning.

By the end of that month the Inspector had grown quieter, and some mornings Elena almost forgot that it was there. The contract, however, had not changed, and it sat on her computer with its wrong number like a stone in a shoe that she had learned to walk around. She had a suspicion that kindness would have something to say about that too, and that she would not enjoy all of it.

On the fifth Thursday Rosa brought sayings from the Jewish, Christian and Muslim traditions to set beside the Buddhist text, and she made a few ground rules before she began. They were to listen with respect, not to rank or compare the traditions, and to correct her at once if she misrepresented anything. Walter and Hana would speak from their own traditions, she said, while she would read the Jewish saying as a respectful guest, because a saying always sounds truest in the voice of someone who loves it.

Walter opened his worn Bible and read the command to love your neighbour as yourself, which first appears in the book of Leviticus and which Jesus, in the Gospels, names as the second of the two greatest commandments. Many teachers have pointed out, he said, that the sentence quietly takes for granted that a person already treats themselves with some care. It measures love for others by love for oneself, and it does not say a word about despising either.

Walter admitted that for most of his life he had read only the first half of the sentence, and that he had worn himself out serving his neighbours while giving himself nothing. Years ago an elderly minister had taken him aside and told him, with a smile, that the text says as yourself and not instead of yourself. Walter said that it had taken him a long time to hear the difference, and that he was still learning it at seventy-three.

Walter turned a few pages and read a line from Psalm 139, in which the writer speaks to God and says that he is fearfully and wonderfully made. He told them that on his hardest mornings he said it aloud to the bathroom mirror, which usually made him laugh, and that laughing was a good beginning. The verse, he said, did not ask anyone to be proud, only to stop insulting what had been so carefully made.

Rosa then read, as a respectful guest, a saying of Hillel, a Jewish teacher of about two thousand years ago, preserved in the Pirkei Avot, a collection of ethical sayings. If I am not for myself, it asks, who will be for me, and if I am only for myself, what am I, and if not now, when? Rosa said that these three short questions seemed to her like a whole philosophy of life, balanced on one foot.

Rosa took the three questions one at a time, slowly, as though tasting each of them. The first says that nobody else can stand on your side in your place, so you must do it yourself, and the second warns that a life lived only for oneself is an empty one. The third, she said, was her favourite, because it refuses to let us put off kindness until we have become perfect enough to deserve it.

Hana told a story from the hadith, the recorded sayings and actions of the Prophet Muhammad, in which a companion named Salman visited his friend Abu Darda and found him exhausted by constant fasting and prayer. Salman urged him to eat and to sleep, saying that his body had a right over him, as his Lord and his family did, and that each should be given its due. When the Prophet heard of it, Hana said, he replied that Salman had spoken the truth.

Hana added that mercy stands at the very front of her faith, because nearly every chapter of the Qur'an begins by naming God as the Compassionate, the Merciful. She said that if mercy is how almost every chapter begins, it seemed strange that so many of the faithful, her loving grandmother included, kept it for guests and never offered it to themselves. She was not sure that this was theology, Hana admitted, but it was what she had begun to think.

Dev asked in his careful way whether all these sayings amounted to the same thing, and Rosa said that she did not think so. Each tradition, she said, has its own reasons, its own words and its own understanding of who we are and what we owe, and it would be unkind to flatten them into one. They were more like songs in different languages that happen to share a tune, and nobody in the circle needed to agree about the words.

That night Elena wrote four words at the top of a clean page in her notebook: on my own side. She could not yet say them aloud without feeling like a liar, and she suspected that being on her own side would take rather more than a sentence, but she underlined them twice anyway. Somewhere under her ribs a very small, stubborn hope had begun to practise standing up.

On the sixth Thursday Rosa wrote two sentences one beneath the other on the whiteboard, and she stepped back to let the circle study them. The first said, I did something wrong, and the second said, I am something wrong, and the difference between them was only a few small words. She asked them to notice how differently each one felt in the body, and the room went very still.

Guilt, Rosa explained, is about the act: it says I did something wrong, and it gives us a job to do, which is to put things right. Shame is about the person: it says I am something wrong, and it gives us nowhere to go except into hiding. Many psychologists distinguish the two in roughly this way, she said, and although the research is still developing, shame seems to make repair harder.

Elena sat very still, because she had just understood something that she did not like. She had not written to Mr Hartley for nearly six weeks, and it was not the figure on page three that had stopped her but the voice that called her a fraud, which made every email feel like a confession. The error was a small thing that could be fixed in ten minutes, and shame had turned it into a mountain by making it about who she was.

Rosa was firm that kindness to yourself does not mean pretending that nothing happened or declaring that everything is fine. A real friend, she said, would not leave you alone with a mistake, and nor would she let you off the hook, but she would sit beside you and help you to mend it. Taking responsibility is therefore not the opposite of self-kindness but one of its strongest forms, and it is also what lets us hold our heads up afterwards.

Rosa offered a recipe for a plain apology, which she said had three ingredients and no garnish. You say what happened, you say that you are sorry, and you say what you will do about it, and then you stop, without a long speech or a dramatic show of suffering. Dev nodded slowly and remarked that the best repairs he had ever done were the ones where he did not make a fuss.

On Friday morning Elena sat down at last to write to Mr Hartley, and the first two drafts were exactly what she feared: long, grovelling and full of self-punishment. She deleted both, put one hand on her heart and spoke to the Inspector, politely, to say that she would take it from here. The third draft came out short and calm, and she was surprised by how quickly the words arrived once she stopped trying to be forgiven in advance.

She corrected the figure to fourteen thousand, checked every other number in the document twice, and attached the new version to the email. In three plain sentences she said what had happened, that she was sorry for the error and that she would be glad to answer any questions. Her finger hovered over the button for a long moment, and then she pressed it, and the message flew off into the evening with a small, ordinary whoosh.

While she waited, the Inspector offered a number of detailed predictions, in which Mr Hartley was furious, the whole firm was in uproar and her name was spoken in the city with a shudder. Elena did not argue with it, and she did not obey it either, but she put on her coat and walked through the autumn park until her legs were tired and her mind had stopped racing. She noticed, somewhere near the pond, that she was breathing a little more deeply than she had in weeks.

Mr Hartley's reply arrived from a hotel abroad the same night, and it was three lines long. He thanked her for catching the mistake and said that he would much rather have it right than quick. He added that he had once ordered four hundred cases of the wrong wine and was still teased about it, and Elena read the message three times, waiting for the sting, and found that there was none.

Elena sat down on the stairs, still holding the phone, and laughed until she had to wipe her eyes. The world had not ended, nobody had shouted, and the thing she had dreaded for nearly six weeks had taken ten minutes and a little courage. She decided that she would tell the circle on Thursday, and that she would also, on the way there, buy Rosa a very large cake.

The relief lasted about a day, and then a great grey tiredness descended, as though someone had pulled out a plug and let all her energy drain away. She lay on the sofa under a blanket at midday, listening to the rain, and it dawned on her that for months she had been working until midnight and calling it dedication. The Inspector arrived promptly to say that she was lazy, and she noticed, with interest, that it never visited when she was rested.

Rosa said at the next meeting that tiredness is one of the critic's best friends, because a weary mind sees threats everywhere and has no energy left to answer back. Poor sleep is known to be closely linked with low mood and irritability, she said, although every person is different and she could only speak in general terms. Kindness, therefore, sometimes looks very unglamorous, like going to bed at ten o'clock with a hot water bottle.

Maeve, who knew the small hours better than anyone, said that the inner critic is at its loudest at four in the morning, when the corridors are quiet and everything seems a little hopeless. Over the years she had made herself a rule, which was never to judge her life, her work or her character at that hour, because the verdict could not be trusted. Walter said solemnly that he would have that rule embroidered on a cushion and sold in the library shop.

Elena decided to run a small experiment and to switch off her light by eleven o'clock every night for a week. On the first evening a thin voice whispered that she had unanswered emails and should be ashamed to be in bed, and she answered, rather grandly, that sleeping was not a crime. By the third night she was drifting off almost before her book had finished its first page, and she woke up feeling oddly pleased to be alive.

The theme the following week was boundaries, and Rosa drew a large circle on the whiteboard with a small gate in the side of it. A boundary, she explained, is not a wall to keep people out but a line that shows where you end and other people begin, with a gate so that you can choose who comes in. Saying no kindly, she said, is not unkindness at all, because it is often the only honest way of saying yes to something else.

Elena confessed that she had a client named Mr Pike, who sent his documents late on Friday evenings and expected them back by Monday morning, and that she had never once said no to him. Walter, who had a hidden talent for theatre, offered to play Mr Pike so that she could practise a kinder and firmer reply. He pulled his chair forward, straightened an imaginary tie and cleared his throat with tremendous menace.

Walter thundered that he was her very best customer, that his business depended on her and that a Monday deadline was a matter of life and death. Elena, trying not to laugh, took a breath, put a hand on her heart and said calmly that she could have it ready by Wednesday but not by Monday. To her amazement the words came out steadily, and the circle applauded as though she had won a prize.

On the very next Friday evening Mr Pike's latest document arrived with its usual demand, and Elena wrote back politely that Wednesday was possible but Monday was not. Her heart thumped as she pressed send, and she half expected the sky to fall in. Mr Pike grumbled in a short reply and then agreed, and she sat looking at the screen with the dazed expression of someone who has walked through a door she had always believed was locked.

Dev admitted, in his dry way, that he had never said no to anybody, which was why his little shop was stacked with a hundred watches and his hands shook by the end of the week. Rosa suggested a sentence with a lot of mercy in it: let me think about it and I will get back to you. Dev wrote it on the back of his hand, and the circle watched him do it with a kind of solemn pride.

Rosa said that every no is also a yes to something else, whether to sleep, to a friend or simply to a quiet weekend. That Friday Elena closed her laptop at six o'clock, left the Pike document where it was and said an enormous yes to a long walk in the park with her phone switched off. The Inspector grumbled from somewhere behind her, but its voice carried less far in the open air, and she did not turn round.

A small hotel in the Douro valley had asked Elena to translate its brochure, and she found herself at midnight rewriting a single paragraph about breakfast for the eleventh time. Every version was perfectly accurate and pleasantly written, and yet each one felt to her like a small act of fraud that somebody would eventually expose. She recognised the pattern, with a sinking feeling, as an old friend of the Inspector's, and its name was perfectionism.

Rosa said that there is nothing wrong with high standards, and that she had no wish to turn anyone into a careless person. The useful question, she said, is whether a standard helps you to do better work or only makes you feel small, because cruelty is a poor teacher of almost everything. Most of us, she noted, produce our finest work when we feel secure enough to risk a blunder.

Rosa told them that in her flower shop not one bouquet had ever been perfect, because there was always a petal turned the wrong way or a stem a little too long. The customers did not notice, and they came back every week for years, because a bouquet that is made with care and finished on time is far more valuable than a perfect one that is never made. A map, she added, does not need to show every leaf on every tree to get you home.

Hana admitted, laughing, that her chemistry notes were the most beautiful in the university and that she had spent far more hours decorating them than learning from them. Her tutor had finally told her that nobody had ever passed an exam by being admired for their highlighters. She now tried to stop when a page was ready rather than when it was flawless, and she said that her grades, to her great surprise, had improved.

This time Elena allowed herself exactly two careful readings, corrected the two real errors she found and sent the brochure off before the Inspector could suggest a third. The hotel owner replied within the hour, in warm and slightly broken English, to say that the breakfast paragraph made her mouth water. Elena sat back, a little dazed, and realised that the eleventh draft of that paragraph had not been better than the first.

One evening, scrolling idly on her phone, Elena came across a post in which a translator she had once met at a conference was holding up a prize, smiling in a golden light. She felt herself shrink within seconds, and the Inspector, which had been waiting for exactly this opportunity, produced a neat chart comparing the two of them in every respect. By the end of it Elena had lost on every point, and her own career looked like a small grey patch on a large bright map.

When Elena confessed her evening of scrolling, Rosa said that we nearly always compare our insides with other people's outsides. We know every doubt and every sleepless night of our own, she said, but of everyone else we see only the prize, the smile and the golden light. It is an unfair contest, and the odd thing is that the winner of the prize is probably, at that very moment, comparing herself with someone else.

Walter passed round a photograph of the tomatoes from his allotment, which glowed red and magnificent in the afternoon sun. Just outside the frame, he told them cheerfully, stood a collapsing shed, a heap of cracked pots and a jungle of weeds that had defeated him for three summers. Every picture of a life, he said, has an edge, and the whole art of envy is forgetting what lies beyond it.

Rosa suggested that envy, though unpleasant, is sometimes a compass, and that we can ask it politely what it is trying to point out. Elena sat with the question for a few minutes and understood, to her surprise, that she did not want the other woman's prize at all. What she wanted, and had wanted for years without admitting it, was to translate books rather than contracts.

That night Elena wrote at the top of a new page: one day I would like to translate a book. She noticed that she had written it as a wish and not as a test, and that the Inspector, usually so quick to point out how unlikely this was, had for once not said a word. She closed the notebook gently, like someone closing the door of a room in which a small plant has just been put on the windowsill.

On her father's birthday Elena phoned him in Porto, hoping to tell him about the hotel brochure and the pleasant letter from its owner. Tomas Costa was an accountant, and he listened in his precise way, asked whether she was still only translating contracts and told her, as he always did, to be very careful. He wished her goodnight in a tone that was not unkind and that landed on her heart like a stone.

Elena felt the sting at once, and her first instinct was to get rid of the feeling as quickly as possible, by scrubbing the kitchen or by answering emails or by shouting at herself. The Inspector joined in with the observation that a grown woman should not be wounded by a phone call, and the effect was to add a second layer of pain on top of the first. She stood there with her arms wrapped around herself, hurt and ashamed of being hurt.

Rosa taught them to make room for hard feelings instead of wrestling with them, much as one makes room on a sofa for a friend who has had bad news. She suggested a simple sentence to say silently to oneself: this hurts, and it makes sense that it hurts. There is nothing to fix at that moment, she said, and nothing to prove, and sometimes simply being accompanied is enough for the pain to soften.

Rosa recalled an old Buddhist teaching that speaks of being struck by two arrows. The first arrow is the pain that life brings, such as a loss, a disappointment or a hurtful word, and nobody can entirely avoid it. The second arrow is the one we fire at ourselves, in the form of blame and self-criticism, and the teaching says that this second arrow, at least, we may learn to put down.

Elena sat at the kitchen table and tried to name exactly what she felt, which turned out to be disappointed, lonely and, underneath that, a little angry. She noticed that the feelings seemed to loosen their grip a fraction as soon as they were named, like knots that are easier to untie when you can see where they begin. Rosa had warned them that naming a feeling is simple but not always easy, and Elena found that she agreed on both counts.

Rosa pinned a card to the wall on which she had written three questions in large, round letters: what am I feeling, what do I need, and what would I say to a friend? They could be asked in any difficult moment, she said, in under a minute, and the answers did not have to be wise or even correct. The point was to turn toward oneself with the same curiosity one would offer to a person one cared about.

That night Elena sat by the window with the card in her hand and asked the questions one at a time. She was hurt, she realised, she needed to feel seen rather than corrected, and to a friend in her position she would have said that her father's words belonged to his own fears and were not a measure of her. It was not a solution, and she did not feel entirely better, but she felt accompanied in her own company, which was new.

Mr Pike returned her Wednesday translation with a long list of corrections, and the note at the top described her work as sloppy. Some of the corrections were fair and some were merely ill-tempered, but the old reflex surged up in her at once, and she wanted to shut the laptop, lie down and give up the profession altogether. The Inspector could not have been more pleased, since someone else was now doing its work for it.

At the circle that week Rosa taught them to pause before answering any criticism and to ask two questions of it, namely what is true and what is useful. That evening Elena drew two columns on a sheet of paper and sorted Mr Pike's list. Two comments were true and useful, three were true but trivial, and the rest were simply the sound of a man in a hurry, and it was oddly calming to discover that criticism could be sifted like flour.

Elena corrected the two real errors, left the rudeness exactly where she had found it and sent a reply that was short, calm and entirely free of grovelling. She noticed that her hands were steady and that the old crash of shame had not come, only a small, clean sense of having done her job. It was, she thought, the first time in her life that she had received a harsh note and had remained, throughout, on her own side.

That Thursday Rosa asked a question that made the room go quiet: whose voice does your inner critic actually sound like? She gave them ten minutes of silence and a pencil, and she added that nobody would be asked to read aloud and that they were free to stop at any moment. Elena looked at the blank page for a long time, and then, to her own surprise, she began to write very fast.

Elena remembered, with a clarity that startled her, a mathematics exam she had failed at the age of fourteen. The paper had come back with a red thirty-one at the top, circled twice by a teacher called Miss Albright, who had written the single word careless beneath it. She could still smell the chalk and the floor polish, and she could still feel the heat rising in her face as the paper was handed back.

That evening at dinner her father studied the paper in silence for what felt like a year, and then he told her, quietly, that she would have to be twice as careful if she wanted a good life. He had not shouted and he had not punished her, and she understood even then that his words were meant as love, from a frightened man who believed that care was the only defence against disaster. But the word careful had gone into her like a splinter, and it had never come out.

Suddenly Elena put down her pencil, because she had seen a connection that took her breath away. On the morning of the contract the very first word the voice had hissed at her was careless, which was Miss Albright's word, delivered in her father's careful tone, more than twenty years after the exam. The Inspector, it seemed, had never written a sentence of its own and had simply been quoting for most of her life.

Rosa said that we all absorb voices as children, from parents, teachers, schoolmates, advertisements and the general mood of the society around us, and that the inner critic often speaks in these borrowed words. Most of the people who lent us those voices, she said, were doing their imperfect best, frightened and tired in their own right. To understand where a voice came from is not to blame anyone, and it is not to excuse everything either, but it loosens the idea that the voice is simply the truth.

Rosa guided them through a short imagining, and she said clearly that anyone could open their eyes and stop whenever it began to feel too heavy. Elena pictured herself as she was now, sitting on a school bench beside the fourteen-year-old girl with the red paper in her hands. The girl did not look up at first, and so Elena simply sat there, patiently, the way one sits with a frightened animal.

In her mind Elena told the girl that one exam could not measure her, and that a thirty-one in mathematics said nothing at all about her heart or her future. She told her that careful people make mistakes too, that it was allowed, and that she was already loved, with or without a perfect paper. The girl looked up at last, and the look on her face was one of enormous, tired relief.

When Elena opened her eyes her cheeks were wet, and the lamplit room seemed to have grown a little brighter. In her notebook she wrote a short note to the girl, saying that she forgave her entirely, that it had never been a crime and that she was sorry it had taken twenty years to say so. It was the sort of note that she had always been able to write to other people, and she read it with the strange feeling of receiving her own mail.

On the way home Elena passed a small sweet shop, and on an impulse she went in and bought a paper bag of the sour cherry sweets that she had loved at fourteen. She sat on a bench in the park beside the pond and ate them one by one, in the cold, in her good coat, and they tasted of being a child. It was, she decided, an entirely sensible thing for a grown woman to do, and she smiled at a passing dog, which looked as if it approved.

That night Elena slept more deeply than she had for months, and in her dream the Inspector stood where it always stood, behind her chair, with its arms folded. It had not gone away, and she did not expect it to, but now she could hear in its voice the schoolroom and the dinner table and the exhausted love of people who had meant well. She woke feeling not victorious but lighter, like someone who has put down a bag she had forgotten she was carrying.

After the meeting Elena stayed behind to help Rosa stack the chairs, and the library grew quiet around them. She had always known that her aunt once ran a flower shop, but it was one of those facts that families keep in a drawer, and she realised that she had never asked what it had really been like. Rosa paused with a chair in her hands, looked at her for a moment and said that she would be glad to tell her.

They sat on two of the stacked chairs, and Rosa described the Green Door, the little flower shop on Mill Lane that she had run for six years. It had buckets of tulips on the pavement, a bell that rang above the door and an old tabby cat asleep among the ribbons in the window. She had loved it with her whole heart, she said, in the way that one loves a place that has made one feel useful.

Rosa said that in those years she had risen at four every morning to buy flowers at the wholesale market and had often locked up long after dark. She was warm and generous with every customer who came through the door, and yet when she pricked her finger on a thorn or forgot an order she called herself names that she would never have used on a stranger. She laughed and admitted that she had once apologised to a rose and then, a moment later, to herself, for apologising.

In the sixth year the landlord raised the rent, and a large supermarket opened nearby and began to sell cheap bouquets by the armful. Rosa tried everything she could think of, from early deliveries to wedding orders, but after a long and difficult winter the accounts would not balance, and she had to put the key through the letterbox for the last time. The empty buckets were taken away on a wet Tuesday, and the cat went to live with a neighbour.

Afterwards, Rosa said, she had treated the closing of the shop as a verdict on her whole character, and she had said to herself things that made Elena's Inspector sound like a polite acquaintance. For almost a year she crossed to the other side of the road so that she would not have to walk past the shuttered window. She was, she said, the very best teacher of this subject, because she had earned the right through years of doing it wrong.

It was her old friend Ada who finally broke the spell, by sitting beside her on a bench one morning with a flask of tea and refusing to leave. She said, very gently, that the shop had ended, but that Rosa had not failed at flowers, and that an ending and a failure were two different things which Rosa had been treating as one. It was the first sentence in a year that Rosa had been able to hear.

In those months Rosa began to spend her days at Millbrook Library, because it was warm and free and nobody there asked her to be cheerful. On a low shelf she found a book about loving-kindness, which she read slowly, over weeks, with a suspicion that slowly turned into relief. A few years later, with the help of Mrs Osei and a borrowed kettle, she began the Thursday circle in the very room where they were now sitting.

Rosa admitted that she still had bad days, especially in March, when the anniversary of the closing came round and the old voice woke up and began to talk. She was not a finished teacher, she said, and she hoped never to pretend to be one, because she was only a person who had been practising for a few more years than anyone else in the room. On those days, she said, she did exactly what she asked of them, and she began again.

Elena had always thought of her aunt as the calmest person in the family, a lighthouse that never wavered, and it was strangely moving to see her as a woman who had once crossed the road to avoid a window. She put a hand on Rosa's arm and said that she was glad to know her better. Rosa patted the hand and said, with a twinkle, that she would be gladder still when the chairs were stacked.

Before they turned out the lights, Rosa took a small paper packet from her coat pocket and pressed it into Elena's hand. It held cornflower seeds, saved from the last summer at the Green Door, and she said that they were not a gift so much as a small experiment in patience. Elena carried them home, scattered them in a pot on her windowsill, watered them once and, being Elena, promptly forgot all about them.

The next theme, Rosa announced, was the plain kindnesses, the ones that nobody puts on a poster. Self-kindness, she said, is not only a warm feeling or a gentle sentence but also a glass of water, a proper meal, a walk in daylight and a bed with clean sheets. A person who speaks tenderly to herself while living on biscuits and coffee, she added, is writing a love letter and then not posting it.

Elena realised with some embarrassment that she often forgot to eat anything until four o'clock, and that she then devoured toast over the keyboard in a state of mild fury. She decided to make lunch a real event, with a plate, a table and the laptop firmly closed, and she put a large glass of water beside her desk where it could not be ignored. Within three days she noticed that her afternoons were less foggy and that the Inspector was less sharp-tongued after soup.

Elena began to take a short walk each morning to the park at the end of her street, without her phone and without any particular destination. She noticed things that she had walked past for years: the colour of the wet leaves, the steam rising from the pond and a robin who sat on the same fence every day and seemed to be waiting for her. It was the first time in months that she had spent twenty minutes doing nothing at all, and the Inspector had been unable to find a single thing to criticise.

Dev reported, in his usual dry way, that he had started to buy himself a proper coffee every Saturday morning and to drink it slowly at a cafe window, watching the world go by. It was the smallest act of kindness he could imagine, he said, and it had taken him forty years to see that he deserved it. He added that he now looked forward to it all week, which he found both pleasant and slightly absurd.

Rosa warned that a life of nothing but sensible habits could turn into another kind of cruelty, and she said that real kindness leaves room for play and for joy. She asked each of them what they had loved to do when they were ten years old, before anyone told them what to be good at. The answers came slowly and then all at once, and the room filled with talk of kites, trains, puddles, secret languages and maps.

Elena remembered that at ten years old she had filled whole notebooks with maps of imaginary towns, complete with harbours, railways and a hospital for dolls. That evening she found a pencil and a sheet of thick paper and drew a map of her own street, with its crooked lamp posts and the pond, and she gave it a compass rose in the corner. It was not useful and it was not good, and she was absurdly, wholeheartedly happy for an hour.

Walter confessed, in a conspiratorial whisper, that for thirty years he had been building model buses in his spare room, and that his masterpiece was a perfect number nine with working doors and a tiny driver. He said that he had always been slightly ashamed of the hobby, as though a grown man ought to spend his time more usefully. Then he grinned and said that he had stopped feeling ashamed on Tuesday, and that the driver had been given a new hat to celebrate.

Hana said that she begins every morning with a short prayer of thanks to God for waking up, and that she had noticed something unexpected about it. For a few seconds, before she looked in the mirror or checked her phone, she felt grateful for her own body, and gratitude left no room in that moment for criticism. Rosa said that she could think of no better description of a plain kindness, and she suggested that those who prayed and those who did not might all learn from it.

Rosa invited them to thank the body for what it does, in place of the usual habit of inspecting how it looks. That evening, in front of the bathroom mirror, Elena felt thoroughly awkward, and she thanked her legs for carrying her to the park, her lungs for the cold air and her stomach for the soup. The Inspector made a small, baffled noise, like an official who has been given a form in a language that he does not read.

Last of all, Elena looked at her hands, which had typed other people's words for almost ten years without a single complaint, except for an occasional cramp. She thanked them out loud, feeling absurd, and then she realised that they were trembling very slightly with something that she could only call tenderness. It was a very small moment, and it changed the way she felt about sitting down to work the following morning.

Elena began to notice a curious side effect, which was that she was becoming more patient with other people. She waited in a long queue at the post office without sighing, held the door for a woman with a pram and found that the usual small irritations of the day slid off her like rain from a coat. It seemed that a person who is less at war with herself has more attention to spare for everybody else.

Her downstairs neighbour, Mrs Pollard, a formidable woman with a fierce hairdo, knocked on the door one evening to complain about the sound of footsteps. In the past Elena would have apologised six times and spent the night rehearsing her shame, but now she listened with real attention, said sorry once and offered to put down a thick rug. Mrs Pollard, who had come armed for a battle, looked quite disarmed, accepted a biscuit and went away smiling.

Over coffee and a very large slice of lemon cake, Marta studied her friend with narrowed eyes and announced that she seemed different, softer somehow and lighter. Elena smiled and said that she was practising being on her own side, which she had never said aloud to anyone, and which sounded less ridiculous in a cafe than it had in her notebook. Marta raised her cup in a toast and said, with great satisfaction, that it was about time somebody was.

Rosa reminded them, rather as a pilot warns of turbulence, that self-kindness is a practice and not a cure. There would be good weeks and terrible weeks, she said, and the terrible ones did not mean that the practice had failed but that a human being was doing it. She asked them to remember this when the day came, because it always came, and she looked very hard at Elena as she said it.

Rosa chalked a tree with deep roots on the blackboard and explained that the word radical comes from the Latin word for root. Radical kindness, she said, is not a bright and showy gesture but a way of going down to the root of how we treat ourselves, and of staying there when we fail at it. Anyone can be kind to themselves on a good day, she added, and it is the bad days that put the roots down.

Then came a crowded week, with three deadlines, a leaking tap and a cold that settled in her chest. On Friday morning Elena dropped her favourite mug, which broke into four pieces on the kitchen floor, and the Inspector returned at full volume, as if it had never been away. It said that she was clumsy, careless and wasting her time with all this kindness nonsense, and that she had learned nothing at all.

Elena spiralled downwards all evening, forgetting the hand on the heart, the three questions and every other tool she owned. Then, at about ten o'clock, she became furious with herself for failing at kindness, which she recognised dimly as the Inspector again, only wearing a new and more spiritual coat. She went to bed feeling that she had thrown away months of progress, and she slept badly.

On Thursday Elena confessed the whole terrible day to the circle, with a rueful little laugh, and she waited for the disappointment that she was sure would follow. Rosa only smiled and said, “Welcome back,” as warmly as if Elena had returned from a long voyage. Beginning again, she explained, is not a failure of the practice but the practice itself, and one does it not once but ten thousand times.

Hana added that the Arabic word for repentance, tawba, carries the sense of returning, and that in her tradition a person is invited to return as often as she needs to. She said that her grandmother used to describe it as a door that is never locked, and that there was something freeing in the idea that the point was not never to leave but always to come back. Elena thought of the robin in the park, which returned to the same fence every morning.

That evening Elena wrote two words on a yellow sticky note, begin again, and stuck it to the edge of her laptop where it could not be missed. She thought that it was the shortest instruction she had ever been given, and perhaps the hardest to follow, and also the easiest to forgive herself for breaking. The mug, glued crookedly together by her own hand, went back on the shelf beside it, and she decided that it looked better with its cracks.

Rosa said that self-kindness has a strong and quiet side, which is the right to protect yourself from people who treat you badly. Being gentle with oneself, she said, is not the same as putting up with everything, and a person who is kind to everyone except those who mistreat her is not being weak but wise. She added that this applies to a boss, a friend or a relative, and that it never requires hatred, only a gate with a good latch.

That night Elena opened her records and looked at her work for Mr Pike with a clear and unhurried eye. He paid late almost every time, his notes were often rude, and in two years he had not once said thank you, though she had met almost every one of his hurried deadlines with a tremor of fear. It was not the Inspector speaking, she noticed, but simply arithmetic, and arithmetic had never once called her a fraud.

Walter, who adored a garden metaphor, said that a good boundary is a gate and not a wall, and that the secret is to keep the latch in your own hand. You open it with pleasure to your friends, he said, and you keep it shut, politely but firmly, against anyone who wants to trample the flowers. Rosa told him that he had just described, in one sentence, an entire week's teaching, and Walter looked extremely pleased with himself.

Elena wrote Mr Pike a short and clear email, and she did not apologise in it once. From now on, she explained, she needed payment within thirty days and at least three working days for every job, and she hoped that this would suit them both. She pressed send with her left hand on her heart, and her right hand, she noticed, was only shaking a little.

Mr Pike replied within the hour, mostly in capital letters, and announced that he would take his work to someone more reasonable. Elena felt a cold wave of fear about money, because he had been one of her regular clients, and underneath the fear, to her surprise, she felt a deep and spacious relief. She made a cup of tea, did her sums honestly and found that she could manage for several months, which was a far calmer calculation than any the Inspector had ever offered her.

Rosa suggested that they try a short sitting each morning, no more than five quiet minutes with the breath and the kind phrases, and she set a small bell on the table to show them how simple it could be. Small and regular, she said, is almost always better than long and rare, because a habit grows from being watered daily and not from a single flood. She asked them to choose a time and a chair and to promise only to turn up.

In the first week of sitting, Elena's mind behaved like a room full of excited puppies, running in all directions and knocking things over. It produced shopping lists, fragments of old arguments, the plot of a film she had not thought of for years and several remarks from the Inspector about her posture. She sat through all of it, five minutes at a time, and she wondered whether she was doing it wrong.

Rosa told her that a wandering mind is perfectly normal, and that the whole of the practice is noticing that it has wandered and coming back, gently, as often as necessary. Then, one grey morning in the second week, nothing special happened at all, and the five minutes passed with a sort of quiet spaciousness that she could not have forced if she had tried. She opened her eyes with the feeling of having rested, not in her bed, but in herself.

Rosa drew five circles, one inside another, and explained that in the traditional practice the good wishes widen in stages. Many teachers describe the order as oneself, then a dear friend, then someone neutral such as the person who sells you your newspaper, then someone difficult, and finally all living beings without exception. She added that nobody is required to reach the outer circles quickly, and that some people spend years in the first.

Elena sent good wishes first to the man at the corner shop, which was easy, and then, with real difficulty, to Mr Pike. She was not required to like him or to forgive him, Rosa had said, and so she chose the smallest phrase that she could honestly mean, which was may you find some peace. To her great surprise, the phrase seemed to land on her as well, as though a window that she had thought was painted shut had opened an inch.

Maeve missed two Thursdays in a row, and her empty chair, with its untouched mug of tea, seemed to take up more room than she ever had. Rosa phoned her on the Friday and asked nothing except whether she would like some company, and the answer, after a long pause, was yes. The next week Maeve came back, thinner in the face and quieter than before, and she asked if she might say something.

Maeve said, in a flat and careful voice, that she had felt very low for many months, and that she had been hiding it at work and at home. The circle had helped her on some days, she said, and the hand on the heart had been a comfort at three in the morning, but none of it had lifted the heaviness. She was not telling them for sympathy, she added, but because she thought she owed the circle the truth.

Rosa thanked Maeve warmly for her courage, and then she said, as she said at the start of every season, that the circle was not therapy and that kindness practices were never a replacement for proper help. Speaking to a doctor, she said, is not a failure of self-kindness but one of its finest expressions, because it means taking your own suffering seriously enough to ask for expert care. She said it slowly and plainly, and she looked at each person in the circle as she said it.

Maeve explained that she had, in fact, already seen her doctor, who had listened carefully and made a plan with her that included regular appointments and some other support. She said that the hardest part had been the first phone call, and that she had put it off for weeks because she felt she ought to cope alone. The circle, she said, was now something good that she did in addition, and not instead.

Rosa wrote a few general signs on the whiteboard, and she stressed that she was not diagnosing anyone: feeling very low for weeks, losing interest in nearly everything, being unable to sleep or eat, or having thoughts of harming oneself. In any of those cases, she said, the right step is to speak to a doctor, a counsellor or someone trusted. If you ever feel in danger, she said, you should call a crisis line or the emergency number in your country straight away, and none of this is shameful, because it is simply what a good friend would urge.

Dev, who rarely spoke without being asked, said in his dry, quiet voice that he had been seeing a counsellor for two years. It had taken him eleven months to make the first appointment, he said, and it was probably the kindest thing that he had ever done for himself. He wished that someone had told him, years earlier, that asking for help was not a sign of a broken watch but of a sensible owner.

At home Elena thought honestly about her own low days, and she was relieved to find that most of them passed within a day or two like weather. She made herself a quiet promise, which she wrote on the back of the sticky note beneath begin again, that if they ever settled in for weeks she would not wait but would speak to her doctor. It seemed to her that this promise was part of being on her own side, in the way that a good roof is part of a house.

At the next meeting Elena asked whether she might tell her own story from the beginning, which she had never done in one piece. She spoke about the wrong number on page three, the voice with its excellent memory, the long weeks of hiding and the short plain email that had ended them. She described the Inspector in such detail that Walter said he felt he had met it, and when she finished she was trembling, but she felt as though she had set something heavy down on a table.

Then, one by one, the others shared their stories, and Walter took a small framed photograph from his coat pocket and set it on the table. It showed his late wife Ruth, laughing in a garden hat, who had spent forty years telling him to be gentle with himself while he politely ignored her. He said, in a voice that was not quite steady, that he had only begun to listen after she died, and that he now heard her every morning in the sound of the kettle.

For a long moment nobody spoke, and the silence in the back room was not empty but full, like a held breath that had at last been released. Then Hana said quietly that she was grateful to every one of them, and Maeve reached across to squeeze Walter's hand. On her way out Elena noticed a new card pinned to the library noticeboard in Rosa's round handwriting, which said that the Thursday circle welcomed new members.

One morning an email arrived from Ms Vane, an editor at Larkfield Press, a small publisher that Elena had admired for years. Mr Hartley, it turned out, had mentioned her name at a dinner, and Ms Vane wondered whether she might be free to translate a short Portuguese novel of about one hundred and eighty pages. Elena read the message three times, and then she went and stood in the kitchen with both hands pressed to her cheeks.

The Inspector arrived within seconds, and it had prepared a full speech: they had chosen the wrong person, she would be found out by the second chapter, and a real translator would have done it in half the time. Elena did not argue with the speech, and she did not obey it, but she put a hand on her heart and breathed slowly until it ran out of words. It struck her as a remarkably efficient use of a single hand, and she very nearly smiled at the Inspector's silence.

That evening she sat down with Rosa's card and asked the three questions about the offer, one at a time. She was frightened and delighted in equal measure, and she needed time, patience and some kind of support. To a friend she would have said that she was capable of it and that there was no shame in asking for help along the way, and the answers did not remove the fear but gave it company.

Rosa told her over tea on a park bench that she would not translate the novel perfectly, because nobody ever has, and that the aim was to do it well and learn as she went. Elena accepted the commission that same afternoon, with a pounding heart and a wide smile. She asked Ms Vane, politely and without apology, for a fair fee and for eight months in place of six, and she received both.

In the first weeks Elena read each chapter aloud before she began, kept a notebook of difficult phrases and worked in short, steady mornings with a thermos of tea at her elbow. She grew fond of the old grandmother in the story, a fierce and tender woman who mended nets and told the truth, and who reminded her more and more of Rosa. Some pages came easily and some fought her, and she tried to greet both kinds with the same courtesy.

One rainy afternoon she was stopped by saudade, the Portuguese word for a tender, aching longing for something or someone absent, which no single English word quite holds. She wrote six versions, each slightly wrong, and she felt the old pull toward the eleventh draft. Then she remembered the hotel breakfast paragraph, chose the least wrong of the six and put a small note beside it for her editor.

A week later Elena was rereading a chapter that she had already sent when she saw it: she had translated a Portuguese saying so that it meant almost the opposite of what the grandmother intended. Her stomach dropped exactly as it had on the morning of the contract, and the familiar heat rose up the back of her neck. The Inspector began to clear its throat in the doorway, and she could feel it getting ready to speak.

This time Elena did not run away from the feeling and did not freeze, and she noticed with a kind of astonishment that she knew exactly what to do. She put one hand on her heart, said silently that this hurt and that it made sense that it hurt, and then thanked the Inspector for its concern and asked it, politely, to wait in the corridor. Two minutes later her heart had slowed, and she could see the mistake for what it was, a sentence that could be mended.

Elena wrote to Ms Vane at once, in three plain sentences, with the corrected passage attached and no grovelling at all. The reply came within the hour, warm and brisk, to say that the copy-editor had already marked the line in pencil and that catching such things was precisely what editing was for. A translator, Ms Vane added, was never meant to work alone, and the whole point of a team was that nobody had to be perfect.

That night Elena sat down at her desk and counted the difference between her two mistakes. The first, which had been tiny, had cost her nearly six weeks of misery, and the second, which had been rather larger, had cost her twenty uncomfortable minutes and a cup of tea. She had not become a person who made no errors, she reflected, but she had become a person who could stay in the room with them, and that was a skill worth having.

Rosa told them that kindness is a practice, and that a practice is like a path across a field of long grass. Nobody makes a path in a single walk, she said, but by going the same way again and again, on good days and bad days, until the grass gives up and the ground becomes clear. The old unkind path, she added, would always be there, but it would slowly grow over if they used the new one.

Walking home through Millbrook Park, Elena noticed for the first time a pale track that cut across the grass between two paved paths. Nobody had planned it, and no council had laid it; it had been worn into the earth by thousands of ordinary people who had each decided, once, to go that way. She stood there for a while in the dusk and thought that this was how a habit of the heart is made, one footstep at a time.

Rosa added, with her usual caution, that many researchers believe repeated practice makes new habits of thought easier to keep, because the brain goes on changing throughout life. How much it changes, and how quickly, is still being studied, she said, and nobody should expect a dramatic transformation in a fortnight. The encouraging part was that every single repetition counted, including the clumsy ones, and especially the ones made on days when it was hard.

Elena decided that a practice she could keep would have to be small enough to fit into a bad day, and she designed her own, with three steps. In the morning she would sit for five quiet minutes, at midday she would say one kind sentence to herself as she would to a friend, and at night she would name one thing for which she could thank herself. It was so modest that the Inspector tried to sneer at it and then found, rather to its confusion, that there was nothing to sneer at.

She copied the three steps onto an index card in her neatest handwriting and propped it against the lamp on her desk, beside the yellow note that still said begin again. The two together looked like a very small and very sincere set of instructions for living, and she was surprised by how seriously she took them. She had spent so many years trying to be flawless that it felt almost daring to aim at being kind.

In a stormy week with a deadline hanging over her, Elena missed two whole days of her practice, and she felt the old scolding rising like damp in a wall. She noticed it, and she named it, and instead of obeying it she sat down on the third morning and began again with no speech at all. It occurred to her that this was probably what Rosa meant by ten thousand times, and that she had just done one more of them.

On Sunday Elena went to Rosa's flat for lunch, and over soup and warm bread she tried to say what the autumn had meant to her. She thanked her aunt for the Thursday circle, for the biscuits and above all for the phone call that had refused to ask any questions. Her voice shook a little, and Rosa, who understood the value of an unhurried silence, simply refilled her bowl.

Rosa shook her head firmly and said that the credit belonged to Elena and not to her. All she had done was hold a door open, she said, and it was Elena who had walked through it, on the days when her legs shook and on the days when she wanted to run home. She added that a teacher who takes the credit for a student's courage has not understood either of them.

Elena phoned her father in Porto and told him about the novel, and she braced herself as she waited for his answer. He began, as usual, by telling her to be careful, and she heard the Inspector stir behind her chair, but she answered gently that she would be careful and also that she was happy. There was a long pause on the line, and then Tomas Costa said, in a voice she had never heard before, that he was proud of her.

That evening, as she drew the curtains, Elena noticed something on the windowsill that she had completely forgotten: the pot of cornflowers. Without any help from her, and in spite of weeks of neglect, the seeds had sprouted into thin, sturdy green plants that leaned toward the glass. She watered them at once, with a rush of guilt that she caught halfway and turned into something gentler, and she told them that they were doing very well.

After Rosa's notice appeared on the board, four new people came to the Thursday circle, and the little back room became crowded and cheerful. Mrs Osei, who had never once complained about the kettle or the noise, carried in extra chairs without being asked and then, to everyone's surprise, sat down on one of them. It was not the largest circle in the world, but it had become a place where a person could arrive tired and leave a little lighter.

Hana asked whether she might lead an evening, and she stood at the whiteboard with unexpected calm to speak about mercy, which is called rahma in Arabic. She said that in her tradition mercy is a quality one is meant to practise and not only to admire, and that it ought to begin at home, which has to include the person who lives inside one's own skin. She finished by saying that her grandmother would have been astonished, and she thought also pleased.

Dev handed Walter a small cardboard box without saying a word, and the circle fell silent. Inside lay Ruth's old wristwatch, which Walter had mentioned in passing weeks earlier as having stopped long ago, and which now ticked quietly on a clean cloth. Dev had not charged him a penny, and he said only that it had been a pleasure to bring something back to life.

For a long moment Walter could not speak, and his big hands, which had steered buses through thirty winters, trembled a little as he took the watch from its cloth. He fastened it to his wrist, where it looked absurdly small, and said that Ruth would have laughed at the sight and then called it an act of kindness towards himself. Then he held it to his ear, listened to the tiny sound, and the whole circle pretended very badly not to be wiping its eyes.

Maeve told the circle that she was feeling steadier these days, that the plan she had made with her doctor was helping and that some mornings were still hard but no longer impossible. She laughed more easily than before, and the circle noticed it and was too wise to mention it. Asking for help, she said, had turned out to be the first real act of being on her own side that she had managed in years.

A new member named Joel, a young father with tired eyes and a cheerful tie, said that he had no idea where to begin. Elena found that she was holding Rosa's card, and she explained the three questions to him slowly, adding that on a hard day one question was enough. She noticed, with some surprise, that her voice was steady and that she meant every single word she was saying.

On the way home Elena realised that explaining the practice to Joel had strengthened it in her own hands, as a path grows firmer with every new traveller. Teaching, she thought, was not the opposite of learning but one of its best forms, provided that one did it with humility and a sense of humour. She decided that she would never be a teacher in the proper sense, only a fellow walker who happened to be a few steps ahead on a particular afternoon.

Rosa told the circle, in her usual unhurried way, that the season would end on the last Thursday before the holidays, and that the room would be closed for a month afterwards. She asked each of them to bring something to the final meeting, not a present or a speech but one small thing that they had learned, which they might say or write or draw. Walter immediately volunteered a model bus, and she told him that this would be perfectly acceptable.

At the last meeting of the season Rosa wrote five short lessons on a large sheet of paper and pinned it to the wall. Pause when the harsh voice starts, rest a hand on your heart, speak as a good friend would, remember that you are not alone, and mend what you can and begin again. They were simple enough to learn in an evening, she said, and deep enough to take a lifetime.

Before they left, Rosa asked each person to write one kind sentence on a folded piece of paper and to pass it to the person on their left, and the room filled with scratching pencils and the smell of tea. Elena's note came from Walter, in his large and wobbly handwriting, and it said that she had made a hard thing look possible. She folded it into her pocket as carefully as she had once folded the letter to herself, and she read it twice more on the walk home.

When they came out of the library the first snow of the winter was falling, soft and slow, and it settled on Walter's cap and on Hana's scarf and in the lamplight on the steps. They hugged one another in the awkward, happy way of people who have told each other the truth, and they promised, all talking at once, to meet again in January. Dev, who rarely said goodbye to anyone at all, said it twice, and then he turned back to say it a third time.

Mr Hartley came home from his long journey in the middle of December and signed the corrected contract without a murmur, and a week later a postcard arrived for Elena, showing a hillside of cork oaks in the Portuguese sun. On the back, in a spidery hand, he had written that he valued honest work above flawless work and that he hoped she would go on translating for him for many years. She propped the postcard against her lamp beside the yellow note, and the figure fourteen thousand had never looked so beautiful.

In the week before the holidays Elena finished the first third of the novel, sixty pages of a fierce and tender grandmother's world rendered, she hoped, into living English. She sent it to Ms Vane with a short note that said it was not perfect but was honest and finished, and she felt a surge of pride that was entirely free of fear. She celebrated with a large bowl of soup and a long walk, because she had learned that celebration was also one of the plain kindnesses.

The next morning, over her tea, Elena found a tiny typo on page eleven of the pages she had sent, and she waited, almost with curiosity, for the old storm to arrive. The Inspector cleared its throat and began its familiar speech, but it sounded rather like an old gramophone in another room, thin and far away and somewhat out of date. She smiled, thanked it for its concern, sent the correction in two lines and went back to her toast with an appetite.

On Sunday afternoon Elena and Rosa walked together along the worn track across Millbrook Park, leaving two lines of prints in the fresh snow. Rosa said that the practice has no finishing line, and that she had stopped waiting for one years ago, because the point was not to arrive but to keep walking in good company. Elena took her aunt's arm and said that this seemed to her the best news she had heard all year.

On the morning after the snow, the first cornflower opened in the pot on Elena's windowsill, a small, ragged, brilliant blue star against the white world outside. It had grown without a grand plan and with only a little water, and she thought that it looked exactly like something that had been given a chance and had simply taken it. She photographed it for Rosa, and then, because it seemed more important, she stood and looked at it for a long time with her own eyes.

That evening, by the light of the lamp and with the blue flower glowing in the dark window behind her, Elena wrote a short letter to the woman she would be in a year's time. She asked for nothing in it, no achievements and no improvements, only that the woman should be warm to herself on the bad days and should remember that they were allowed. Then she sealed the envelope, wrote the date on the back and put it in the top drawer, beside the first letter.

Lying in bed that night, Elena thought about the word radical and its Latin root, and about the trees in the park whose branches were bare and whose roots she could not see. Everything she had learned that autumn, the hand on the heart, the three questions, the plain apology and the gate with its latch, seemed to grow from a single root, which was simply to be on her own side. It was a root that went down further than success or failure, she thought, and it was still there on the days when she forgot it.

That night Elena found a card from Rosa tucked inside her bag, written in the round handwriting that she now knew almost as well as her own. It said that the Buddhist, Jewish, Christian and Muslim sayings they had shared were only small windows onto very large and living traditions, which she should explore in their own words. It said, too, that no card and no circle could take the place of a doctor, a counsellor or a good friend when the weight was heavy.

These days, when Elena makes a mistake, the voice she hears in her head is warm, steady and wise, and it sounds remarkably like her aunt's. She has not become perfect, and she no longer believes that she should be, for she has found something much better in the radical, quiet decision to be on her own side.
